Day 1
From Hotel: 25 min → Jama Masjid
1.Jama Masjid
India's largest active mosque, completed in 1656 under Shah Jahan, its central courtyard holds up to 25,000 worshippers at Friday prayers; the eastern minaret's 130-step climb gives the widest rooftop view over the rooflines of Old Delhi.

2.Red Fort
The 17th-century Mughal fortress of red sandstone from which India's Prime Minister addresses the nation on Independence Day, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with palaces, pavilions, and a sound-and-light show by night.

From Hotel: 12 min → India Gate
1.India Gate
The 42-metre triumphal arch on Kartavya Path commemorating the 70,000 Indian soldiers killed in World War I; the Eternal Flame of the National War Memorial burns beneath it around the clock.

3.Jantar Mantar
The 1724 open-air astronomical observatory built by Maharaja Jai Singh II, its masonry instruments — including a sundial accurate to within two seconds — are still used for stellar observation.

1.Hauz Khas
A 14th-century royal reservoir ringed by Feroz Shah Tughlaq's madrasa, mosque, and tomb; the ruins sit above a deer park with open rooftop views across the water, and the village lane below is lined with galleries and cafés.

The 73-metre sandstone minaret begun in 1193 — the world's tallest brick minaret — UNESCO World Heritage Site surrounded by a complex of mosques, tombs, and an iron pillar that has not rusted in 1,600 years.

1.Akshardham
The Swaminarayan Akshardham temple completed in 2005, its central monument carved from 234 ornate pillars of pink sandstone; the exhibitions inside trace 10,000 years of Indian culture. No cameras or electronics permitted inside.

A 90-acre landscaped park enclosing the 15th-century tombs of the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties — domed mausoleums surrounded by birdwatching trails and joggers, a calm contrast to the city's monuments.

3.Gandhi Smriti
The former Birla House where Gandhi spent his final 144 days; the museum traces his life across 11 rooms and the garden marks with a footpath the exact route he walked to his assassination on 30 January 1948.

24 min · 8 min → Bangla Sahib
4.Bangla Sahib
Delhi's most prominent Sikh gurudwara, built on the site where Guru Har Krishan stayed in 1664; its golden dome reflects in the sarovar pool, and its langar serves free meals around the clock to anyone who arrives — one of the largest community kitchens in the city.

Local Tastes
Butter Chicken
Delhi's most famous export, invented at Moti Mahal in Daryaganj in the 1950s — tender chicken in a velvety tomato-cream sauce, best eaten with naan. The original restaurant still operates on Netaji Subhash Marg near Daryaganj.
Moti Mahal · Daryaganj
Chaat
Street snacks built on contrasting layers — golgappa, aloo tikki, and papdi chaat. Chandni Chowk has the oldest chaat vendors in the city; the narrow lanes around Paranthe Wali Gali are the most concentrated stretch.
Chandni Chowk · Old Delhi
Kulfi
Dense, slow-frozen Indian ice cream in flavours of pistachio, saffron, and rose — richer and less airy than Western ice cream; sold on sticks or in clay cups throughout Old Delhi and Connaught Place.
Old Delhi · Chandni Chowk area
Nihari
A slow-cooked meat stew — beef or mutton — simmered overnight with whole spices, eaten for breakfast in Old Delhi; Karim's near Jama Masjid has served it since 1913 and remains the city's best-known address for it.
Karim's · Jama Masjid
Food Delivery
Swiggy
Foreign number: not accepted. — Swiggy requires an Indian mobile number; the sign-up form does not accept international country codes.
Delhi's leading food delivery platform with the widest restaurant network — Old Delhi kebab kitchens to Connaught Place chains. Delivery windows run 30-45 minutes; coverage extends across the full NCR region.
swiggy.com
Zomato
Foreign number: not accepted. — Zomato requires an Indian mobile number; international numbers are rejected at sign-up.
Matches Swiggy's Delhi coverage and often runs steeper discounts; doubles as Delhi's most comprehensive restaurant discovery tool with photos, ratings, and menus. Pro membership unlocks free delivery across the city.
zomato.com
Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted. — International numbers accepted at sign-up; SMS verification arrives for +1, +44, and most major country codes within a minute.
Uber covers all of Delhi and the NCR region. UberAuto and UberMoto cost a fraction of standard cars for short hops; surge pricing is common during evening peak hours and monsoon rains.
uber.com
Ola
Foreign number: accepted. — The form accepts international country codes; SMS codes arrive for most major countries within 2-3 minutes.
Ola is Uber's main rival in India and is often cheaper, with broader coverage in outer Delhi neighbourhoods. The app includes auto-rickshaws, bike taxis, and a cash payment option — useful if you prefer not to link a foreign card.
olacabs.com

Day Trips by Train
Agra · 1 hr 40 min
Taj Mahal · Agra Fort · Fatehpur Sikri. A full day covers the Taj at sunrise and Agra Fort before the return train; the Taj is best before 9am as crowds peak by mid-morning.
🎫 book at: irctc.co.in or Omio
Jaipur · 4 hr 30 min
Amber Fort, Hawa Mahal, City Palace, and Jantar Mantar are all within auto-rickshaw distance of the station; the bazaars in the old walled city — textiles, lac bangles, blue pottery — are best in the afternoon.
🎫 book at: irctc.co.in or Omio
Worth Knowing

Start early — the best Delhi is before 9am

Every major monument is quieter and better-lit in the first hour after opening. The Qutb Minar complex and Humayun's Tomb are nearly empty before 8am; by 10am both can be crowded with school groups. The November-January smog period sees air quality drop sharply — an N95 mask is worth packing if your visit falls in that window.

The Delhi Metro covers most of this itinerary cheaply. The Yellow Line runs through Rajiv Chowk · Connaught Place · to Chawri Bazar for Old Delhi. A stored-value Metro card costs ₹100 deposit and rides are ₹10-60 depending on distance.

Remove shoes at every mosque, gurudwara, and many temples before entering; carry a small bag or use the free shoe racks provided. Jama Masjid and Bangla Sahib provide free head coverings at the entrance — head covering is required for women at both. Akshardham enforces a strict dress code: shorts, sleeveless tops, and short skirts are not permitted; fabric wraps are available at the gate at no charge.
